newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan airport chaos as controllers go slow.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan airport chaos as controllers go slow.

text.p: An air traffic controllers go-slow crippled Kenya's main airports on Saturday, stranding tourists and other passengers as international airlines were forced to re-route flights, airport officials said.

Up to 400 air traffic controllers at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA) in the capital, Moi International Airport in Mombasa, Kenya's second city and the centre of its tourism industry and at other airports, started the action at midnight on Friday (2100 GMT), air officials said.
The strike put increased pressure on a government rocked by an International Monetary Fund (IMF) decision on Thursday to halt a big aid package to Kenya.
The IMF suspended a $205 million three-year loan citing concerns over corruption and reform of the energy sector.
Tourism is Kenya's biggest hard currency earner with 717,000 visitors in 1996.

"There are 300-400 on the go-slow across the country. The grievance is just remuneration, better pay and working conditions. It's a very rich industry but we are not being paid highly," an air traffic controller coming off shift told Reuters.

The go-slow delayed airport traffic for hours at JKIA, forcing at least six international flights to land in Mombasa, while others re-routed to Kilimanjaro Airport, north Tanzania. Domestic flights were also grounded, passengers said.

A total of 374 passengers on a Friday British Airways flight from London were stranded at Mombasa on Saturday afternoon after circling JKIA for an hour on Saturday morning before heading for the coastal airport, one passenger said.
The delays were expected to worsen late on Saturday when the airport is usually jammed with international flights.
Hundreds of frustrated passengers milled around JKIA departure lounge, many complaining a lack of official information irritated them as much as delays.
"We are not aware there is a strike," a Civil Aviation official was quoted on Kenya Television Network as saying.
"They (airport authorities) told us the flight was delayed due to weather conditions. Half an hour later they told us there were problems in the operational tower," said a passenger.
Air traffic controllers said they would not resume normal work until government met their demands and warned that pilot fatigue, after time spent circling, could endanger safety.
"We realise how the passengers and captains feel, these are people we know. We would like help from the airlines to put in a word for us to the government," one controller said.
Tourism operators said the strike would hurt business, reducing the flow of valuable European and American customers.

"We have been here since early this morning waiting for passengers to come from the U.S. This is terrible if this strike goes on it could kill the tourist industry," said Francis Ombuni of Park East Safaris.
Air traffic controllers, transport ministry employees barred from belonging to trade unions, staged a five day strike last December causing long delays at Nairobi and Mombasa airports.

The controllers now say government has failed to keep a pledge to raise pay after January 31 and say their starting salary is equivalent to $90 a month, well below levels paid by international aviation authorities.
